title: the Purusha Sukta
hook: a festival crowd seen from above is all heads, hands and feet. the Purusha Sukta opens with a person like that, and bigger than the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of the Nasadiya Sukta: the one in highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps does not know. Did you say how far you'd seen, and no further? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

A festival crowd, photographed from a rooftop. At first it looks like one thing, a single moving surface. Then you zoom in. Heads, thousands of them. Hands in the air. Feet, sandals, a child on someone's shoulders. It's one crowd and it's countless people, and you can't quite say where one ends and the next begins. The Rig Veda has a hymn that opens on a picture something like that, except the crowd is one person, and the person is bigger than the world. After a hymn that asked who knows, here is one that begins by describing. Today: the Purusha Sukta.
screen: `A CROWD FROM A ROOFTOP.` → `ONE THING, COUNTLESS PEOPLE.` → `NOW MAKE IT ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Purusha means person, a man, a human being. Earlier on this path the word meant the quiet seer in the Yoga Sutras. Here, in the Rig Veda, it names a cosmic person. The hymn opens: sahasra-shirsha purushah. The Purusha has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. Some readers hear thousand as a way of saying beyond counting: every head is in some sense his, every pair of eyes, every step. Then the first verse says he covered the earth on every side, and stood beyond it by ten fingers' width. That small measure is strange and lovely. Not by a mountain or an ocean. By ten fingers. As if to say: he holds the whole world, and there is still a little more of him past its edge. Verse two widens it further. Purusha eva idam sarvam. The Purusha is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be. Past and future, in one person. Hold those two verses together and the picture has a double edge. The Purusha is everything there is, and also more than everything there is. Inside the world, and just past its rim. Teachers of different Hindu schools read its person in their own ways. For today, stay with the opening picture. Every face in that rooftop crowd, and a little beyond it.
screen: `PURUSHA: A PERSON.` · `A THOUSAND HEADS, EYES AND FEET.` · `BEYOND THE EARTH BY TEN FINGERS.` · `ALL THIS, WHAT HAS BEEN AND WILL BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel a little past your own edge. Sit, and rest your hands on your knees or in your lap. Feel the hands from the inside: warmth, weight, a faint tingle. Now let your attention go to the air just past your fingertips, a few inches out. You can't touch it, but you can sense it, the room continuing. Rest there: the body, and a little more. When your mind wanders, come back to the fingertips, and then just past them. If you pray, you can rest in prayer there. The bell holds the time.
The Purusha Sukta. The hymn of the cosmic person: a thousand heads, eyes and feet, all that has been and will be, and still ten fingers more. Today's word.
Your line: the Purusha Sukta. Today, in one crowd, a line, a train car, a room, look at the faces as one picture, and then as each one. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is a hymn of the Rig Veda that Hindus recite in worship and in traditional Vedic chanting, and teachers of different schools quote and interpret it.

fork.setup: you're the poet. the Purusha covers the whole earth. how far beyond it does he reach?
options: not at all: he is exactly the world
fork.reveal: the first verse says he stood beyond the earth by ten fingers' width: the whole world, and a little more.

original.note: Sanskrit: a person, a human being. In Rig Veda 10.90 it names the cosmic person.

trapdoor: what you thought: purusha is a technical word for the self in yoga.
what it means: in the Rig Veda it's a cosmic person with a thousand heads, eyes and feet, filling the world and going beyond it.
what a scholar hears: sahasra-shirsha purushah, sahasrakshah sahasrapat, and the strange measure dashangulam, ten fingers' width beyond the earth.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.90.1 (the Purusha has a thousand heads, eyes and feet; he covered the earth on every side and stood beyond it by ten fingers' width)
Yoga Sutras 4.18 (purusha as the unchanging seer), referenced from an earlier day

notes: First Purusha Sukta day (1256–1261): verses 1–2. Following days take verses 3–4, 6–10, 11–12, 13–14 and 15–16.

Sanskrit given from memory in simplified transliteration: 1a sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt; 1d atyatiṣṭhad daśāṅgulam; 2a puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam (written open as purusha eva idam sarvam for reading). Confirm.
'About the width of two hands laid side by side' is the writer's gloss on daśāṅgulam; some read it as an idiom for 'beyond'. Confirm or cut.
'Some readers hear thousand as a way of saying beyond counting': offered as a reading, not the text's claim; confirm.
'Recited in worship and quoted by teachers from very different schools': general; confirm or soften. No claim is made about its place in any particular ritual.
The Yoga Sutras link refers back to the year-four Yoga Sutra days (purusha as seer, 4.18).
Editor: cut the writer's unsourced measurement gloss of ten fingers' width and the sweeping claim about the hymn's use in worship and across schools.
